questions.q: In the retail store example, what makes an employee more valuable to the company?
a: Handling difficult customers well
Refilling shelves quickly
Working longer hours
Knowing all product prices
questions.why: From the lesson on surviving the dip, the retail store example contrasts replaceable shelf-refilling with valuable difficult-customer handling.

questions.q: According to the International Ice Cream Association, what percentage of U.S. ice cream sales does vanilla account for?
a: Almost 30%
About 15%
Roughly 20%
Nearly 40%
questions.why: From the lesson on being the best, the book cites the International Ice Cream Association for vanilla at nearly 30 percent of U.S. sales.

questions.q: What does Zipf's law describe in the context of the book?
a: The large gap in results between first and second place
The rate at which new businesses fail
The time needed to master a skill
The cost of entering a new market
questions.why: From the lesson on being the best, Zipf's law is introduced to explain the large gap between first and second place results.

questions.q: How does the book distinguish smart quitting from failing?
a: Smart quitting is a conscious choice; failing is running out of options
Smart quitting means giving up early; failing means trying too hard
Smart quitting avoids risk; failing embraces it
Smart quitting is for small businesses; failing is for large ones
questions.why: From the lesson on identifying when to give up, the book frames smart quitting as a conscious choice versus failing as running out of options.

questions.q: In the figure skating example, what represents the dip?
a: The long practice needed to learn jumps
The initial excitement of gliding on ice
The first time falling on the ice
The decision to stop skating
questions.why: From the overview, the figure skating analogy shows the dip as the long slow slog of learning jumps after initial gliding excitement.
